item.content:encoded:
The South African Master in Ocean Sciences (AOS-SAMOS) is an innovative postgraduate programme designed to strengthen Ocean Sciences education, research capacity and professional opportunities in South Africa while supporting the sustainable development of the country’s growing Blue Economy.

The programme brings together nine South African universities, national research institutions and European academic partners to create an internationally recognised, interdisciplinary Master’s degree that combines ocean science, marine biology, oceanography, quantitative analysis, digital technologies, social sciences, law, humanities and sustainability.

Applications for the 2027 AOS-SAMOS cohort are currently open, with a maximum intake of 30 students. The application deadline is Sunday, 31 August 2026.

What Is the South African Master in Ocean Sciences?

The South African Master in Ocean Sciences is a collaborative postgraduate initiative developed in response to the increasing importance of oceans and coastal environments to South Africa’s economy, environment and society.

South Africa faces a range of interconnected challenges affecting its marine and coastal systems, including:

  • Climate change and global warming
  • Biodiversity loss
  • Overfishing and over-exploitation of marine resources
  • Coastal development and urbanisation
  • Environmental degradation
  • Water-quality challenges
  • Sustainable fisheries and food security
  • Marine conservation
  • Environmental governance
  • The need for better scientific data and forecasting
  • The sustainable development of the Blue Economy

These challenges require professionals who can understand the ocean from multiple perspectives rather than from a single academic discipline.

AOS-SAMOS therefore provides an interdisciplinary training environment in which students can develop the scientific, analytical, research, digital and professional skills needed to contribute to modern Ocean Sciences and sustainable development.

The programme is also designed to strengthen collaboration between South African universities and European partners while improving postgraduate teaching and research capacity, particularly at Historically Disadvantaged Universities (HDUs).

Why Was the SAMOS Programme Created?

South Africa has significant marine and coastal resources, but there has historically been limited access to comprehensive, interdisciplinary postgraduate education in Ocean Sciences.

The SAMOS project was created to address this gap by bringing together the expertise and infrastructure of universities and research institutions across South Africa.

The programme seeks to:

  1. Modernise postgraduate Ocean Sciences education in South Africa.
  2. Improve the quality and relevance of higher education in Ocean Sciences.
  3. Increase graduate employability.
  4. Prepare professionals capable of addressing major environmental and socioeconomic challenges.
  5. Strengthen teaching and research capacities at Historically Disadvantaged Universities.
  6. Build stronger networks between South African and European universities.
  7. Establish a major centre of Ocean Sciences expertise in the Eastern Cape.
  8. Support research and innovation relevant to the sustainable Blue Economy.
  9. Promote inclusive and interdisciplinary education.
  10. Contribute to Sustainable Development Goals relating to education, gender equality, climate action, life below water, equality and global partnerships.

The programme is supported through the Erasmus+ Capacity Building in Higher Education framework and is co-funded by the European Union under Grant Agreement No. 101179091.

A Truly Interdisciplinary Ocean Sciences Programme

One of the major strengths of AOS-SAMOS is its interdisciplinary approach.

Rather than limiting students to one narrow area of marine science, the programme integrates different fields that are increasingly important for understanding and managing marine and coastal systems.

The curriculum brings together areas including:

  • Physical oceanography
  • Chemical oceanography
  • Marine biology
  • Applied marine biology
  • Operational oceanography
  • Marine social sciences
  • Environmental sustainability
  • Law and humanities
  • Earth observation
  • Satellite oceanography
  • Quantitative analysis
  • Scientific programming
  • Bioinformatics
  • Geographical Information Systems
  • Data visualisation
  • Marine conservation
  • Environmental monitoring
  • Research methodology
  • Professional and collaborative skills

The programme is intentionally interdisciplinary and Afro-centric, with an emphasis on applying Ocean Sciences to challenges relevant to South Africa and the wider African region.

Programme Structure

The AOS-SAMOS degree is a full-time taught Master’s programme worth 180 credits.

It consists of:

  • 90 credits of coursework
  • 90 credits for a minor dissertation

The programme is scheduled to commence in February 2027 for the 2027 cohort. The coursework component is expected to run over approximately 24 weeks between February and August 2027 at the Nelson Mandela University Ocean Sciences Campus in Gqeberha. Students are required to attend the coursework in person.

Depending on the funding and study pathway, the degree can be completed over one or two years.

Students receiving SAMOS-NRF funding follow a two-year curriculum, allowing the dissertation component to be completed during the second year. Self-funded students may have the option of following a 13-month pathway with the minor dissertation at the University of Cape Town.

Where Will Students Study?

Applications for the 2027 programme are managed through a single-entry point at the University of Cape Town (UCT).

The coursework is delivered at the Nelson Mandela University Ocean Sciences Campus in Gqeberha, Eastern Cape.

Students subsequently undertake their minor dissertation through one of the participating South African partner universities, depending on their research area and supervisory arrangements.

The Ocean Sciences Campus provides access to specialised facilities, research infrastructure and a network of researchers working across marine and environmental disciplines.

Facilities and research entities associated with the campus include areas such as:

  • Marine and coastal research
  • Marine robotics
  • Environmental observation
  • Coastal palaeosciences
  • Marine and fisheries research
  • Maritime education and research
  • Environmental monitoring
  • Hyperbaric research infrastructure

This gives students the opportunity to combine classroom-based postgraduate education with practical research and exposure to real-world marine science.

What Will Students Learn?

The curriculum is designed to prepare graduates for professional and research careers across the Ocean Sciences sector.

Students are expected to develop the ability to:

  1. Apply a whole-systems approach to sustainability in an ocean sciences context.
  2. Understand regional marine ecosystems and their dynamics.
  3. Collect and analyse Ocean Sciences data using quantitative techniques.
  4. Develop and conduct research projects addressing theoretical or practical problems.
  5. Apply advanced analytical and computational tools.
  6. Work with models and data relevant to Ocean Sciences.
  7. Use emerging technologies and tools in marine research.
  8. Monitor environmental change and assess the impacts of human activities.
  9. Examine sustainable development across different economic sectors.
  10. Analyse emerging threats and opportunities affecting ocean sustainability.
  11. Work effectively in multidisciplinary teams.

These skills are intended to prepare graduates for both research-oriented and professional careers in the Blue Economy.

Key Areas of the Curriculum

1. Applied Ocean Sciences

The programme provides students with a broad foundation in applied Ocean Sciences, enabling them to understand how marine systems operate and how scientific knowledge can be applied to real-world environmental and socioeconomic challenges.

2. Marine Biology

Students can develop knowledge relevant to marine organisms, ecosystems, biodiversity and the management and conservation of marine resources.

3. Operational Oceanography

Operational Oceanography focuses on observing, understanding and predicting marine conditions.

Students are introduced to the use of satellite observations, in-situ measurements and numerical models to generate information that can support decision-making in science, government and industry.

4. Earth Observation and Satellite Oceanography

Earth Observation provides tools for monitoring marine environments on large spatial scales.

Students explore concepts including satellite sensing, electromagnetic radiation, ocean-light interactions and the use of remote sensing technologies for understanding marine environments.

5. Advanced Data Analysis

The programme also provides training in advanced analytical and computational techniques.

Depending on the area selected, students may work with:

  • Bioinformatics
  • Geographical Information Systems
  • Multivariate analysis
  • Scientific programming
  • Satellite oceanography
  • High-performance computing
  • Advanced data visualisation

Students gain practical experience applying these tools to real datasets.

6. Minor Dissertation

The 90-credit minor dissertation allows students to undertake substantial research in a selected area of Ocean Sciences.

Students may conduct their research across different disciplines offered by the SAMOS partner universities and are generally based at the university of their principal supervisor.

Applicants seeking NRF funding are required to identify a potential supervisor and research project before submitting their funding application.

Who Can Apply?

AOS-SAMOS is designed for qualified postgraduate applicants who have an academic background relevant to the programme.

The programme welcomes applicants from both natural sciences and social sciences/humanities, although preference is given to applicants with a strong science background and demonstrated numerical skills.

Previous specialised knowledge of oceanography or marine biology is not essential.

Applicants should generally have:

  • A four-year Bachelor’s degree that includes a research project; or
  • An Honours degree; or
  • Another equivalent NQF Level 8 qualification;
  • The qualification must include a 30-credit research component and demonstrate disciplinary alignment with the AOS-SAMOS curriculum;
  • An average of at least 65% in science subjects, or above 70% in other pertinent subjects;
  • A strong academic record;
  • A demonstrated interest in marine science;
  • Good numeracy skills are strongly recommended.

Applicants without a natural sciences background must explain in their motivation letter how they intend to address gaps in natural science and numerical knowledge.

Can Applicants Without a Science Degree Apply?

Yes.

This is one of the distinctive features of AOS-SAMOS.

The programme does not restrict eligibility exclusively to traditional marine science, oceanography or biology graduates.

Applicants from social sciences and humanities backgrounds can be considered, provided they meet the relevant academic requirements.

However, applicants without a natural sciences background are expected to demonstrate how they will compensate for gaps in science and quantitative knowledge.

This makes the programme potentially relevant to graduates whose previous studies include areas such as environmental policy, economics, development studies, law, governance, geography, social sciences and related disciplines, subject to the programme’s academic requirements and disciplinary alignment.

English Language Requirements

English is the language of instruction and examination.

Applicants must provide evidence of English-language proficiency.

For South African applicants, acceptable evidence includes the relevant English qualification through the National Senior Certificate or Senior Certificate.

International applicants can demonstrate English proficiency through recognised tests such as:

  • TOEFL
  • IELTS
  • National Benchmark Test Academic Literacy

The published requirements include a minimum IELTS overall band score of 7.0, with no individual component below 6.0.

For TOEFL, the stated minimums include:

  • 570 for the paper-based test
  • 230 for the computer-based test
  • 88 for the internet-based test

Applicants should check the official requirements before applying because documentation and testing requirements can vary depending on individual circumstances.

International Applicants

The programme is not restricted exclusively to South African citizens.

The official requirements page provides a pathway for international applicants, including applicants from outside South Africa.

International applicants must satisfy the academic and English-language requirements and must also contact the University of Cape Town’s International Academic Programmes Office for guidance on the documentation required to study in South Africa.

The programme therefore has potential relevance to applicants from across Africa and beyond, although admission is competitive and subject to the stated academic requirements and available places.

How Competitive Is the Programme?

AOS-SAMOS has a maximum intake of 30 students for the 2027 cohort.

This means applicants should not treat meeting the minimum academic requirements as an automatic guarantee of admission.

Applicants should prepare a strong application that clearly demonstrates:

  • Academic achievement
  • Interest in Ocean Sciences
  • Relevant experience
  • Research interests
  • Career objectives
  • Understanding of the programme
  • Quantitative and analytical ability
  • Potential research direction
  • Ability to work collaboratively

The motivation letter is particularly important because it gives applicants an opportunity to explain their academic background, experience, reasons for applying and research interests.

Application Documents

Applicants should prepare the required supporting documentation carefully.

The official application guidance lists:

  • Curriculum Vitae, limited to two pages
  • Proof of highest qualification
  • Academic transcripts
  • Motivation letter
  • Relevant information concerning academic background and experience
  • Research interests
  • Identified supervisor and research project where applicable

Applicants applying for the SAMOS-NRF bursary must identify a potential supervisor and research project before applying for the funding.

They may also need to provide a reference letter from a current supervisor, course convenor or Head of Department addressing academic performance, research ability, reliability, professionalism, disciplinary history, readiness for Master’s-level study and ability to work in a collaborative environment.

Incomplete applications will not be considered.

Application Deadline

For the 2027 AOS-SAMOS Master’s programme, applications are currently open and will close on:

Sunday, 31 August 2026

There are only 30 available places, making it important for prospective applicants to submit complete applications before the closing date.

Important Funding Deadline

The programme application and funding application are separate processes.

For the 2027 academic year, applicants seeking the DSTI-NRF Master’s Student Funding were invited to apply through NRF Connect by the UCT internal closing date of 26 June 2026.

The SAMOS programme website states that 10 bursaries are available through this call, subject to NRF eligibility requirements and funding decisions. Acceptance into SAMOS does not automatically guarantee funding.

Therefore, applicants should distinguish between:

  • The AOS-SAMOS programme application deadline: 31 August 2026
  • The 2027 DSTI-NRF funding deadline: 26 June 2026

Applicants who are specifically interested in funding should check the latest official funding information rather than assuming that admission automatically includes a scholarship.

Funding and Financial Support

AOS-SAMOS is not automatically a fully funded Master’s programme for every admitted student.

The programme provides information about several potential funding sources, including the DSTI-NRF Master’s Student Funding scheme and other postgraduate funding opportunities.

South African students and permanent residents may be considered for Full Cost of Study or Partial Cost of Study funding, subject to the relevant eligibility criteria and availability of funding.

International students may qualify for Partial Cost of Study funding, although the number of international scholarships is limited.

The programme therefore encourages applicants to investigate multiple funding sources and to consider self-funding where necessary.

Programme Fees

The published 2026 fee structure provides an indication of the programme’s costs.

For South African students, the stated total is approximately R78,300, consisting of coursework and dissertation fees.

For SADC students, the published total is approximately R83,900, including the applicable administrative fee.

For non-SADC African students, the published total is approximately R132,100.

For international students from outside Africa, the published total is approximately R148,400.

These figures are based on the published fee information and should not be assumed to be the final 2027 fees. The programme advises applicants to check the updated fee information for the relevant academic year.

Accommodation

Students are expected to attend the coursework component physically at Nelson Mandela University’s Ocean Sciences Campus in Gqeberha.

Accommodation is the responsibility of successful students.

Nelson Mandela University provides assistance to students looking for suitable off-campus accommodation, but applicants should plan their accommodation and living expenses separately from tuition and other academic costs.

Career Opportunities After the Programme

The AOS-SAMOS programme is designed to improve graduate employability and prepare students for careers connected to the sustainable Blue Economy.

Potential areas of employment and professional development include:

  • Oceanography
  • Marine biology
  • Marine conservation
  • Environmental consulting
  • Coastal management
  • Fisheries and marine-resource management
  • Environmental monitoring
  • Ocean observation
  • Satellite and Earth Observation
  • Marine data analysis
  • Scientific programming
  • Marine policy
  • Environmental governance
  • Research institutions
  • Government agencies
  • Non-governmental organisations
  • Maritime and ocean-related industries
  • Sustainability and environmental consulting
  • Academic and research careers

The programme’s emphasis on interdisciplinary knowledge, quantitative skills, digital tools, research and professional collaboration is intended to help graduates respond to both scientific and socioeconomic challenges within the Blue Economy.

Why the Programme Matters for Africa

Africa’s oceans represent an enormous source of economic, environmental and social potential.

Marine ecosystems support fisheries, tourism, transport, coastal communities, food systems and other economic activities. At the same time, these systems are increasingly threatened by climate change, biodiversity loss, pollution, unsustainable exploitation and poorly managed development.

Building a highly skilled generation of African ocean professionals is therefore essential.

AOS-SAMOS contributes to this objective by creating a postgraduate training environment that connects scientific knowledge with policy, technology, conservation, business and sustainable development.

The programme’s focus on collaboration between South African institutions and European partners also provides an opportunity to strengthen international academic networks and research cooperation.

A Strong Opportunity for Interdisciplinary Graduates

A particularly important aspect of AOS-SAMOS is that applicants do not necessarily need to come from a conventional marine science background.

The programme recognises that solving complex ocean problems requires people with different perspectives.

A graduate with a strong background in science may contribute advanced technical knowledge, while someone from the social sciences, humanities, law, policy or another related field may contribute expertise in governance, human behaviour, economics, policy or societal impacts.

This multidisciplinary approach reflects the reality that ocean challenges cannot be solved through science alone.

How to Apply

Prospective applicants should begin by reviewing the official AOS-SAMOS admission requirements and preparing their supporting documents.

The application process involves:

  1. Reviewing the eligibility requirements.
  2. Preparing a suitable CV of no more than two pages.
  3. Obtaining proof of the highest qualification.
  4. Preparing complete academic transcripts.
  5. Writing a strong motivation letter.
  6. Clearly explaining academic and professional experience.
  7. Describing research interests.
  8. Selecting preferred study streams.
  9. Identifying a prospective supervisor and research project if applying for SAMOS-NRF funding.
  10. Submitting the application through the University of Cape Town’s application system.
  11. Ensuring all supporting documents are submitted.
  12. Completing the application before the 31 August 2026 deadline.

Applicants should carefully verify all requirements before submission because incomplete applications will not be considered.

Study Streams

Applicants applying through UCT are instructed to select the relevant Master’s qualification and choose their preferred stream.

The two listed options are:

  • Applied Ocean Sciences (Applied Marine Biology)
  • Applied Ocean Sciences (Operational Oceanography)

Applicants are required to indicate their first and second choices during the application process.

Key Facts at a Glance

Feature Details
Programme South African Master in Ocean Sciences (AOS-SAMOS)
Level Master’s degree
Cohort 2027
Duration One or two years depending on pathway
Credits 180 credits
Coursework 90 credits
Dissertation 90 credits
Maximum intake 30 students
Start date February 2027
Main coursework location Nelson Mandela University Ocean Sciences Campus, Gqeberha
Application entry point University of Cape Town
Study mode Full-time
Instruction language English
Study areas Ocean Sciences, marine biology, oceanography, data analysis, sustainability and related fields
Application deadline 31 August 2026
Funding Separate funding opportunities available; not automatically guaranteed
Programme support Erasmus+ / European Union co-funded project

Final Thoughts

The South African Master in Ocean Sciences (AOS-SAMOS) represents a major investment in the future of Ocean Sciences education, research and professional development in South Africa.

By bringing together nine South African universities, research institutions and European partners, the programme offers an unusually collaborative approach to postgraduate education. Its combination of marine science, oceanography, data analysis, Earth Observation, sustainability, research and professional skills makes it relevant to the increasingly complex challenges facing oceans and coastal communities.

The programme may be particularly attractive to graduates who want to build careers in marine science, environmental sustainability, conservation, ocean observation, research, consulting, policy or the wider Blue Economy.

For prospective students interested in the 2027 cohort, the most important date to remember is 31 August 2026, when applications close. Because the programme has a maximum intake of only 30 students, applicants should prepare their documents carefully and submit a complete application before the deadline.

The programme is also a reminder that the future of sustainable development will increasingly depend on professionals capable of connecting scientific knowledge with policy, technology, economics, conservation and society.

For applicants passionate about oceans and interested in building advanced interdisciplinary expertise, AOS-SAMOS could provide a valuable pathway into the growing field of Ocean Sciences and the sustainable Blue Economy.

Official application information: AOS-SAMOS Requirements and Registration

Official programme website: South African Master in Ocean Sciences (AOS-SAMOS)

item.content:encoded:
The National Lottery Community Fund is a major source of community funding in the United Kingdom, supporting projects designed to help people connect, develop, overcome disadvantage and create stronger communities.

Through funding generated by the National Lottery, the organisation supports community-led initiatives that seek to make a meaningful and lasting difference to people’s lives. Its overall focus is on building stronger, fairer and more inclusive communities, with particular attention given to people experiencing poverty, disadvantage or discrimination.

The National Lottery Community Fund has set an ambitious long-term goal: by 2030, it plans to distribute more than £4 billion to help create stronger and fairer communities across the UK.

This makes the fund an important potential source of support for organisations, community groups and initiatives working to address social, economic, environmental and wellbeing challenges.

Rather than focusing on only one type of project, the organisation supports a broad range of community-led activities. These can include initiatives that bring people together, improve outcomes for children and young people, strengthen physical and emotional wellbeing, protect the environment and help communities respond to climate change.

What Is The National Lottery Community Fund?

The National Lottery Community Fund is the UK’s largest community funder, distributing money raised through National Lottery funding to support projects that benefit communities.

Its approach is strongly centred on community-led change. This means that the organisation backs projects developed around the needs, priorities and aspirations of local communities.

The fund’s work is based on the understanding that communities can create better outcomes when people have opportunities to:

  • Build meaningful connections with one another.
  • Reduce isolation and loneliness.
  • Create welcoming and inclusive community spaces.
  • Support children and young people to thrive.
  • Improve physical, mental and emotional wellbeing.
  • Protect nature and the environment.
  • Respond to environmental challenges and climate change.
  • Address poverty, disadvantage and discrimination.
  • Develop stronger and more resilient communities.

For organisations seeking community funding in the UK, understanding these priorities is important because successful projects are expected to demonstrate how their work can contribute to positive outcomes for people and communities.

National Lottery Community Fund’s Long-Term Vision

The organisation’s overarching vision is built around the belief that stronger communities create brighter futures.

Its funding strategy therefore places community-led initiatives at the centre of its work. Rather than simply providing financial support, the fund aims to contribute to broader social change by investing in projects that can improve people’s experiences and strengthen communities.

By 2030, the National Lottery Community Fund intends to share over £4 billion to help build stronger and fairer communities throughout the United Kingdom.

This long-term commitment creates significant opportunities for community organisations and groups whose projects align with the fund’s priorities.

The Four Community-Led Missions

The National Lottery Community Fund has identified four major community-led missions that guide the outcomes it wants to see from the projects it supports.

These missions provide an important framework for understanding the types of projects that may be relevant to its funding programmes.

1. Communities Come Together

The first mission focuses on helping communities become more connected, welcoming and inclusive.

Social connection is an important part of building healthy communities. Projects under this broad area can help people develop relationships, participate in community activities and feel that they belong.

The fund highlights outcomes such as:

  • Building stronger connections between people.
  • Reducing loneliness and social isolation.
  • Creating spaces where people feel welcome.
  • Encouraging participation in community activities.
  • Helping people develop stronger relationships within their communities.
  • Creating opportunities for people from different backgrounds to interact and work together.

Community organisations working to tackle loneliness, isolation or social exclusion may therefore find this mission particularly relevant.

The emphasis is not simply on bringing people together for individual events. The broader objective is to create stronger and more connected communities where people feel included and able to participate.

2. Communities Help Children and Young People Thrive

The second mission focuses on babies, children and young people.

The National Lottery Community Fund recognises that communities can play an important role in helping younger people grow, connect and build positive futures.

Projects in this area may seek to improve opportunities and outcomes for children and young people by helping them:

  • Develop relationships and social connections.
  • Participate in positive community activities.
  • Access supportive environments.
  • Build confidence and skills.
  • Feel connected to their communities.
  • Develop healthier and brighter futures.

Organisations working with children, young people and families should therefore consider how their proposed project could demonstrate meaningful and measurable benefits for its participants.

3. Communities Are Healthier

The third mission focuses on community health and wellbeing.

Health is considered broadly within this mission, including physical, mental and emotional wellbeing.

Projects can contribute to healthier communities by creating opportunities for people to become more active, improve their wellbeing, access supportive environments and develop healthier lifestyles.

Potential areas of relevance include:

  • Physical wellbeing.
  • Mental wellbeing.
  • Emotional wellbeing.
  • Community-based health initiatives.
  • Activities that encourage healthier lifestyles.
  • Programmes that help people participate in supportive social environments.
  • Initiatives designed to improve overall community wellbeing.

Projects addressing health and wellbeing challenges should clearly explain the problem they are responding to and demonstrate how their activities could result in positive outcomes for the people involved.

4. Communities Are Environmentally Sustainable

The fourth mission focuses on environmental sustainability and the ability of communities to respond to environmental challenges.

The National Lottery Community Fund is interested in projects that can help communities protect nature, reduce environmental harm and respond to climate change.

Relevant initiatives may include projects focused on:

  • Protecting nature.
  • Improving local environments.
  • Reducing environmental harm.
  • Community sustainability.
  • Responding to climate change.
  • Encouraging environmentally responsible behaviour.
  • Helping communities become more resilient to environmental challenges.

This means environmental and climate-focused community projects may be able to align with the fund’s sustainability priorities where they demonstrate clear community benefits.

Who Can Benefit From The Funding?

The National Lottery Community Fund is focused on community projects rather than personal financial support for individuals.

Its funding is intended to support initiatives that create positive outcomes for people and communities across the UK.

The organisation places particular emphasis on supporting people experiencing:

  • Poverty.
  • Disadvantage.
  • Discrimination.
  • Social isolation.
  • Other barriers that can prevent people from participating fully in community life.

A strong project proposal should therefore demonstrate a clear community need and explain how the proposed activities will address that need.

Applicants should also show that their project is genuinely connected to the community it intends to serve.

Where Is The Funding Available?

The National Lottery Community Fund operates across the United Kingdom.

Its website identifies four geographical funding areas:

  1. England
  2. Northern Ireland
  3. Scotland
  4. Wales

However, applicants should not assume that every funding programme has identical geographical eligibility requirements.

Different programmes can have different rules concerning location, applicant type, project size, eligible activities and funding amounts.

Applicants should therefore check the specific requirements of the programme they intend to apply for before preparing a full application.

What Types of Projects Could Be Relevant?

Because the National Lottery Community Fund operates multiple funding programmes, the precise activities supported can vary.

Nevertheless, the organisation’s four missions provide a useful indication of the broad areas in which community projects may have potential relevance.

Examples of potentially relevant project themes include:

Community connection projects

These may include initiatives designed to:

  • Reduce loneliness.
  • Bring residents together.
  • Build community relationships.
  • Create inclusive spaces.
  • Encourage participation.
  • Support people who are socially isolated.

Children and youth projects

These may include initiatives that:

  • Support young people.
  • Improve community participation.
  • Provide positive activities.
  • Build confidence and connections.
  • Help children and young people develop.
  • Strengthen support networks for younger people.

Health and wellbeing projects

These may include programmes focused on:

  • Physical activity.
  • Mental wellbeing.
  • Emotional wellbeing.
  • Healthy lifestyles.
  • Community-based wellbeing.
  • Social activities that contribute to healthier communities.

Environmental projects

These may include initiatives focused on:

  • Nature conservation.
  • Community environmental action.
  • Climate change.
  • Sustainability.
  • Reducing environmental damage.
  • Improving local natural spaces.

These examples should be treated as broad areas of alignment rather than a guarantee that a particular activity will qualify for funding. Applicants should always check the eligibility criteria for the specific funding programme.

Why Community Organisations Should Consider This Funding

The scale and breadth of the National Lottery Community Fund make it a potentially important funding source for eligible community initiatives across the UK.

One of the major advantages is that the organisation does not focus on a single social issue.

Instead, its four missions cover several areas that are central to community development:

  • Social connection.
  • Children and young people.
  • Health and wellbeing.
  • Environmental sustainability.

The fund also has a strong focus on communities experiencing poverty, disadvantage and discrimination.

This makes it particularly relevant to organisations that are developing projects to address real community needs rather than simply seeking funding for general organisational expenses.

How To Find The Right National Lottery Community Fund Programme

The National Lottery Community Fund provides a dedicated section where applicants can browse its funding programmes.

This is an important stage of the application process because there is not necessarily one universal grant application that applies to every organisation or project.

Applicants should review the available programmes and filter them according to relevant criteria.

When looking for a suitable programme, consider:

  1. Your project’s location
    Confirm that your project operates in an eligible part of the UK.
  2. The type of organisation applying
    Check whether the programme accepts your particular organisation or community group structure.
  3. The people your project supports
    Clearly identify who benefits from your work.
  4. The community problem you are addressing
    Explain why the project is needed and what challenge it seeks to solve.
  5. Your project’s objectives
    Establish what you want to achieve through the funding.
  6. The relevant community mission
    Consider whether your project contributes to stronger connections, better outcomes for children and young people, healthier communities or environmental sustainability.
  7. The programme’s individual requirements
    Read the full eligibility rules, application guidance and funding conditions before applying.

Preparing A Strong Application

Getting ready before beginning an application can significantly improve the quality of a funding proposal.

The National Lottery Community Fund provides guidance designed to help applicants understand the funding process and complete applications with greater confidence.

Before applying, organisations should consider preparing the following information.

A clear description of the project

Explain what the project is, what activities will take place and how the project will operate.

Avoid describing the idea only in general terms. Give the funder a practical understanding of what will happen if funding is awarded.

Evidence of community need

Explain the problem that the project is designed to address.

A strong proposal should answer questions such as:

  • What problem exists?
  • Who is affected?
  • Why is the issue important?
  • What evidence demonstrates the need?
  • Why is the proposed project an appropriate response?

Clearly identified beneficiaries

Explain who will benefit from the project.

This may involve identifying a particular community, age group or population experiencing disadvantage, isolation, poverty or another challenge.

Expected outcomes

Explain what will change as a result of the project.

For example, a project may aim to increase community participation, reduce loneliness, improve wellbeing, help young people develop stronger connections or increase community involvement in environmental sustainability.

A realistic implementation plan

Show how the project will be delivered.

This can include:

  • Key activities.
  • Project stages.
  • Staffing or volunteers.
  • Community partners.
  • Resources required.
  • Monitoring and evaluation.
  • Expected timescales.

A realistic budget

Applicants should carefully consider how much funding is needed and how the money will be used.

A clear budget helps demonstrate that the proposed project has been thoughtfully planned.

The Funding Journey

The National Lottery Community Fund describes the funding process as a journey that moves from an initial idea through application and, if successful, into delivery of the funded project.

The organisation provides guidance across several stages.

Stage 1: Develop your idea

Start by identifying a genuine community need and developing a project that responds to it.

Stage 2: Get ready to apply

Review the available guidance and determine which funding programme best fits the project.

Stage 3: Submit an application

Complete the relevant application process and provide the requested information.

Stage 4: Wait for the funding decision

The application will be considered according to the relevant programme’s requirements and assessment process.

Stage 5: Start the funded project

If funding is awarded, the organisation can begin delivering the approved activities in accordance with the grant conditions.

Stage 6: Manage and report on the funding

Successful applicants may need to report on progress, demonstrate how funding has been used and communicate the impact of their work.

This means receiving a grant is not the end of the process. Funded organisations have responsibilities for managing the funding and demonstrating progress.

APPLY HERE 

Visit the National lottery fund website HERE

More grants, visit the OFY Website HERE

Managing Your National Lottery Community Fund Grant

The National Lottery Community Fund also provides support for organisations that have already received funding.

This can include guidance relating to:

  • Managing the grant.
  • Reporting project progress.
  • Promoting funded work.
  • Making the most of the grant.
  • Meeting funding requirements.

Successful organisations should therefore ensure that they understand their responsibilities after receiving funding.

Keeping accurate records, monitoring activities and documenting outcomes can help organisations demonstrate the impact of their project.

Important Funding Priorities

Applicants should pay particular attention to the organisation’s emphasis on poverty, disadvantage and discrimination.

These issues form an important part of the fund’s wider purpose.

A project is likely to be stronger when it can clearly demonstrate:

  • The community challenge it is addressing.
  • The people affected by that challenge.
  • Why those people need support.
  • How the project will respond.
  • What positive outcomes are expected.
  • How the community will be involved.
  • How the results will be measured.

Community-led approaches are particularly important because the fund’s strategy places local people and communities at the centre of its work.

Government Consultation On National Lottery Funding

The National Lottery Community Fund’s website also highlights a UK Government consultation concerning how National Lottery funding should support communities across the UK.

The government is seeking public views on how this funding should be distributed.

The National Lottery Community Fund encourages people interested in community funding to learn more about the consultation and have their say.

This is separate from applying for a grant, but it provides an opportunity for people and organisations interested in community development to contribute to discussions about the future direction of National Lottery funding.

Latest News From The National Lottery Community Fund

The organisation’s website also features updates and stories relating to community funding.

Recent examples listed on the provided page include:

Have Your Say On How National Lottery Funding Is Distributed

Published: 27 July 2026

This update provides information about the government consultation on how National Lottery funding should support communities across the UK.

Support That Saved Me – Sam’s Story

Published: 22 June 2026

This story highlights the experience of Sam and her family and the support they received from Home-Start Wrexham during a difficult period.

Community Is Our Superpower – Israel and Kowther’s Stories

Published: 22 June 2026

This story focuses on Belfast City of Sanctuary and its work supporting refugees, asylum seekers and newcomers in Northern Ireland.

The Solidarity Fund: £60 Million Awarded To Tackle Root Causes Of Poverty, Disadvantage And Discrimination

Published: 9 June 2026

This update discusses almost £60 million awarded to organisations through the Solidarity Fund, with a focus on addressing the root causes of poverty, disadvantage and discrimination.

These updates demonstrate the range of community issues being addressed through National Lottery Community Fund-supported initiatives.

Is There A Deadline To Apply?

No single deadline is stated on the information provided.

This is important because the page presented is the main National Lottery Community Fund website rather than a single grant programme with one application closing date.

The organisation has multiple funding programmes, and individual programmes may have different:

  • Opening dates.
  • Closing dates.
  • Application windows.
  • Eligibility criteria.
  • Funding amounts.
  • Assessment procedures.

Applicants should therefore identify the specific programme that fits their project and check its individual deadline before submitting an application.

Do not assume that a deadline associated with one National Lottery Community Fund programme applies to all funding opportunities.

How To Improve Your Chances Of Submitting A Strong Proposal

Although eligibility and assessment criteria depend on the individual funding programme, applicants can take several practical steps when preparing a community funding proposal.

1. Start with the community need

Do not begin with the amount of money you want.

Begin by explaining the problem affecting the community and why action is needed.

2. Put the community at the centre

Because the fund places strong emphasis on community-led missions, demonstrate how local people have influenced, shaped or will participate in the project where applicable.

3. Be specific about outcomes

Instead of simply saying that a project will “help the community”, explain exactly what positive changes you expect to achieve.

4. Connect the project to the relevant mission

Clearly demonstrate how your project contributes to one or more of the National Lottery Community Fund’s four missions.

5. Demonstrate inclusion

If your project supports people experiencing disadvantage, poverty, discrimination or isolation, explain this clearly and show how the project will remove barriers to participation.

6. Create a realistic budget

Request an amount that is appropriate for the project’s activities and clearly explain how the funding will be used.

7. Read the programme-specific guidance

This is one of the most important steps.

The overall National Lottery Community Fund strategy provides broad direction, but the exact requirements for an application depend on the particular funding programme.

How To Access National Lottery Community Fund Opportunities

Applicants interested in community funding should explore the organisation’s funding programmes and identify the opportunity that best matches their project.

The website provides dedicated sections for:

  • Getting ready to apply.
  • Funding programmes.
  • Managing funding.
  • Application portal.
  • The organisation’s strategy.
  • Community missions.
  • Regional funding information.
  • Contact and support.

Applicants can also access information relating to funding in England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales.

Key Takeaways

The National Lottery Community Fund represents a major opportunity for eligible UK community organisations and groups seeking financial support for projects that create positive social, health, youth or environmental outcomes.

The most important points to remember are:

  • It is a community grant funding opportunity.
  • The fund supports projects across the United Kingdom.
  • Its long-term ambition is to distribute more than £4 billion by 2030.
  • The organisation focuses particularly on communities affected by poverty, disadvantage and discrimination.
  • Funding is guided by four community-led missions.
  • These missions focus on community connection, children and young people, health and wellbeing, and environmental sustainability.
  • Funding is intended for community projects rather than personal financial assistance.
  • Funding programmes may have different eligibility criteria and deadlines.
  • No universal deadline is provided on the main information supplied.
  • Applicants should identify the specific funding programme relevant to their project before applying.
  • Successful applicants are expected to manage their grants responsibly and report on project progress.

Conclusion

The National Lottery Community Fund offers an important funding route for community-led projects across the UK. With a long-term commitment to distributing more than £4 billion by 2030, the fund has positioned community development, inclusion and social impact at the heart of its strategy.

Its four community-led missions provide a clear indication of the types of positive change it wants to support: bringing communities together, helping children and young people thrive, creating healthier communities and promoting environmental sustainability.

For organisations considering an application, the strongest starting point is to identify a genuine community need, understand the people who will benefit, develop a practical project and demonstrate the outcomes the project intends to achieve. Applicants should then compare their idea against the available funding programmes and carefully review the specific eligibility requirements, application guidance and deadline for the programme they choose.

Because there is no single deadline stated on the main information provided, applicants should avoid relying on general funding dates and instead check the individual programme before submitting an application.

For community organisations across England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales, the National Lottery Community Fund can be an important source of support for initiatives seeking to create stronger, healthier, more inclusive and environmentally sustainable communities.

item.content:encoded:
The City of Boston is inviting qualified candidates to apply for the Special Projects Fellow position within the Office of Youth Engagement and Advancement (OYEA) under the Department of Human Services. This is a one-year rotating, full-time position designed for an organized and proactive professional who is interested in public service, youth development, civic engagement and community-based initiatives.

The opportunity provides successful applicants with the chance to work directly on projects designed to strengthen youth participation in decision-making and connect young people with resources and opportunities across Boston. The Fellow will collaborate with city departments, schools, community organizations and other stakeholders while supporting a variety of seasonal and rotating projects.

According to the official City of Boston job posting, the position has one opening, is based at the Central Office, pays $25 per hour, and involves 35 hours of work per week. The application deadline is January 29, 2027.

About the City of Boston Special Projects Fellow Position

The Special Projects Fellow will work within the Office of Youth Engagement and Advancement, an office focused on ensuring that young people have meaningful opportunities to participate in decisions and initiatives that affect their lives.

OYEA works across three interconnected areas of youth development:

  1. Spaces and programmes for young people—supporting environments and initiatives where young people can learn, participate and develop.
  2. Adults and professionals working with young people – strengthening the capacity of youth workers and other professionals who support Boston’s youth.
  3. Young people themselves – creating opportunities for youth leadership, participation, civic engagement and community development.

The Fellow will therefore have an opportunity to contribute to initiatives that operate across these three areas rather than being restricted to one specific project.

The position is particularly suited to someone who enjoys coordinating projects, communicating with different stakeholders, working with communities and managing multiple responsibilities simultaneously.

What Makes This Opportunity Important?

The Special Projects Fellow will contribute to initiatives intended to empower young people to become community leaders and agents of change.

The City of Boston’s youth engagement approach recognizes that young people should not simply be recipients of services. Instead, they should have opportunities to participate in conversations, programmes and decisions that influence their communities.

As a result, the Fellow will work in an environment where activities can involve the following:

  • Youth engagement and outreach
  • Civic education
  • Community partnerships
  • Public service initiatives
  • Youth programmes
  • Focus groups and listening sessions
  • City-wide events
  • Outreach campaigns
  • Resource connections
  • Community development
  • Interagency collaboration

The role also requires meaningful engagement with diverse communities throughout Boston.

Key Responsibilities of the Special Projects Fellow

The successful candidate will undertake a broad range of project coordination, administrative, communication and community engagement responsibilities.

1. Project Management and Coordination

One of the central responsibilities will be overseeing rotating and seasonal projects within OYEA.

The Fellow will help move projects from planning through implementation and follow-up. This includes keeping track of:

  • Project timelines
  • Deliverables
  • Follow-up activities
  • Implementation requirements
  • Project documentation
  • Stakeholder responsibilities
  • Shared resources

This makes project management skills particularly valuable for applicants.

2. Maintaining Project Documentation

The Fellow will be expected to maintain organized project files, documentation and shared resources.

Strong organizational skills will therefore be important because the position involves managing multiple initiatives and ensuring that relevant information can be easily accessed by colleagues and partners.

3. Building Relationships With Stakeholders

The position involves active communication and relationship-building with a wide range of stakeholders.

These may include:

  • City agencies
  • Community organizations
  • Schools
  • External partners
  • Youth-serving organizations
  • Community stakeholders

The purpose of these relationships is to support youth-focused initiatives and strengthen collaboration between the City and organizations working with young people.

4. Supporting Youth Engagement

The Fellow will assist with meaningful youth engagement activities.

This can include participating in or supporting:

  • Direct youth outreach
  • Focus groups
  • Listening sessions
  • City-wide events
  • Youth engagement activities
  • Community meetings
  • Representation activities

Applicants should therefore be comfortable interacting directly with young people and communities.

5. Supporting Logistical Activities

The role also has an important administrative and logistical component.

The Fellow may assist with:

  • Purchasing
  • Reserving spaces for activities
  • Outreach campaigns
  • Event logistics
  • Other operational requirements associated with OYEA projects

This means candidates should be comfortable handling practical details in addition to broader programme responsibilities.

6. Tracking Budgets and Procurement

The Fellow will also support financial and procurement-related administration.

Responsibilities include helping to track:

  • Project budgets
  • Invoices
  • Procurement requirements

This work will be carried out in coordination with OYEA staff. Applicants with experience handling project budgets, invoices or administrative records may therefore have an advantage.

7. Supporting Language Access

The position includes helping connect speakers of languages other than English with available translation and language services.

This is particularly relevant to the City’s goal of meaningful engagement with diverse communities.

Applicants who have experience working across language or cultural differences may find this aspect of the position especially relevant.

8. Professionalism and Accountability

The Fellow must demonstrate professionalism, discretion and accountability when interacting with:

  • Young people
  • Community organizations
  • City employees
  • External partners
  • Other stakeholders

Because the role involves working with youth and public-sector partners, sound judgment and responsible handling of information are important.

9. Staff Development and Training

The Fellow will participate in the following:

  • Staff meetings
  • Training activities
  • Professional development opportunities

The position is therefore not limited to day-to-day project execution; it also provides exposure to professional development within a municipal government environment.

Minimum Qualifications and Requirements

Applicants should carefully review the eligibility requirements before applying.

Professional Experience

The City of Boston requires a minimum of two years of full-time experience or equivalent part-time experience.

Relevant experience could include work involving:

  • Project coordination
  • Youth programmes
  • Community engagement
  • Public service
  • Administration
  • Civic engagement
  • Stakeholder coordination
  • Event coordination
  • Outreach
  • Programme implementation

Bachelor’s Degree

A Bachelor’s degree is strongly preferred.

The official posting also states that a bachelor’s degree may be substituted for the two years of required experience. Applicants should therefore carefully assess their combination of academic qualifications and professional experience when determining their eligibility.

Bilingual Skills

Being bilingual is preferred.

Although bilingual ability is not listed as an absolute requirement, applicants who can communicate effectively in more than one language may be particularly well positioned for a role that includes connecting speakers of languages other than English with translation and language services.

Youth Engagement

Applicants should be capable of serving as positive role models for young people and engaging constructively with diverse communities.

This is a particularly important aspect of the position because the Fellow will participate directly in youth engagement and community activities.

Interest in Public Service

The City is looking for candidates with an interest in areas such as

  • Public service
  • Civic engagement
  • Youth services
  • Youth programmes

Applicants should demonstrate a genuine interest in improving opportunities and resources available to young people.

Organizational and Attention-to-Detail Skills

Strong attention to detail and organizational ability are required.

This is important because the Fellow will simultaneously manage projects, documentation, stakeholders, logistics, budgets and other administrative responsibilities.

Ability to Manage Multiple Projects

Candidates must be able to work on multiple projects simultaneously.

Applicants should therefore be prepared to demonstrate their ability to prioritize competing responsibilities, meet deadlines and maintain quality while handling several assignments.

Communication Skills

Excellent oral and written communication skills are required.

Strong communication will be important when working with city agencies, schools, community organizations, young people and other stakeholders.

Microsoft and Google Workspace Skills

Applicants should be proficient with:

  • Microsoft applications
  • Google Suite

Familiarity with common office productivity tools will help the successful candidate manage documentation, communication and project-related tasks.

Driver’s Licence

A driver’s licence is preferred.

It is not identified as an absolute requirement in the posting, but it may be useful because the position involves off-site travel.

Work Schedule and Location

The Special Projects Fellow is a regular, full-time position based at the City of Boston’s Central Office.

The position requires 35 hours per week and pays $25 per hour.

Applicants should also be aware that the role requires a degree of scheduling flexibility. Some activities may take place during:

  • Evenings
  • Weekends
  • Off-site locations

The posting specifically states that off-site travel is required.

Fellowship Duration

The City of Boston describes the position as a one-year rotating position.

This means the successful Fellow will spend approximately one year supporting a variety of projects and initiatives rather than being assigned permanently to a single programme.

This structure can provide broad exposure to youth engagement, municipal government operations, project management and community partnerships.

Boston Residency Requirement

One of the most important eligibility conditions is that Boston residency is required.

This is a critical requirement for prospective applicants outside Boston.

Therefore, international candidates, including applicants from African countries such as Kenya, should not assume that they can apply simply because they meet the educational and professional requirements. The official posting explicitly requires Boston residency.

Background Checks

The position requires both:

  • C.O.R.I. check
  • S.O.R.I. check

These checks are part of the hiring requirements for the position.

Applicants should therefore be prepared to undergo the applicable background screening process if selected.

Salary and Employment Terms

The advertised employment terms include:

  • Position: Special Projects Fellow
  • Department: Human Services
  • Office: Office of Youth Engagement and Advancement
  • Employment: Regular full-time
  • Duration: One year
  • Openings: 1
  • Workweek: 35 hours
  • Pay: $25 per hour
  • Location: BCC003 – Central Office
  • Employment classification: Non-Union
  • Residency: Boston residency required
  • Background checks: C.O.R.I. and S.O.R.I. required

Who Should Apply?

This opportunity is particularly relevant to professionals who have experience or strong interest in:

  • Youth development
  • Community engagement
  • Civic participation
  • Public administration
  • Public service
  • Programme coordination
  • Project management
  • Stakeholder engagement
  • Community outreach
  • Youth services
  • Event coordination
  • Communications
  • Education and civic programmes

Candidates who can demonstrate strong organizational skills, communication ability, attention to detail and the ability to coordinate several activities at once may be particularly competitive.

Who Is Eligible to Apply?

The official requirements indicate that eligible candidates should generally have:

  1. At least two years of full-time or equivalent part-time professional experience, unless the experience requirement is satisfied through the degree substitution provision.
  2. A Bachelor’s degree, which is strongly preferred and may substitute for the required two years of experience.
  3. An ability to work positively with young people and diverse communities.
  4. An interest in public service, civic engagement and youth programmes.
  5. Strong communication and organizational skills.
  6. Ability to manage multiple projects.
  7. Proficiency in Microsoft applications and Google Suite.
  8. Ability to work flexible schedules, including some evenings and weekends.
  9. Ability to travel off-site.
  10. Boston residency, which is explicitly required.

Bilingual ability and a driver’s license are preferred but are not listed as mandatory qualifications.

Can International Applicants Apply?

This is an important distinction.

The City of Boston states that Boston residency is required. Therefore, the opportunity should not be treated as an open international fellowship that applicants from any country can freely apply for.

The posting also states that the City of Boston is an equal opportunity employer and that qualified applicants are considered regardless of characteristics including race, sex, age, religion, colour, national origin, ancestry, disability, marital status, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and veteran status, among other protected categories.

However, this equal-opportunity statement does not remove the separate Boston residency requirement.

For applicants living outside Boston, especially those based in other U.S. states or other countries, the residency requirement should therefore be carefully considered before submitting an application.

How to Strengthen Your Application

Applicants should tailor their application materials to the actual responsibilities of the role rather than submitting a generic resume.

Highlight Project Management Experience

Show specific examples of projects you have coordinated from planning through implementation.

Where possible, demonstrate:

  • The project objective
  • Your responsibilities
  • The stakeholders involved
  • The timeline
  • The resources managed
  • The results achieved

Demonstrate Youth or Community Engagement

If you have worked with young people, schools, community organizations or youth-serving programmes, make this experience prominent.

Examples might include:

  • Youth programmes
  • Community outreach
  • Workshops
  • Civic education
  • Mentorship programmes
  • Community events
  • Focus groups
  • Listening sessions

Emphasize Stakeholder Coordination

Demonstrate your ability to work with multiple organizations or groups.

For example, explain how you coordinated government departments, schools, NGOs, community organizations, private-sector partners or other stakeholders to achieve a common objective.

Show Organizational Ability

Because the role involves multiple projects, documentation and logistical responsibilities, applicants should demonstrate that they can manage competing priorities effectively.

Use concrete examples rather than simply stating that you are “organized.”

Highlight Communication Skills

The position requires excellent oral and written communication.

Your application should therefore demonstrate experience with:

  • Professional correspondence
  • Reports
  • Presentations
  • Outreach campaigns
  • Stakeholder communication
  • Public engagement
  • Community communications

Mention Digital Skills

Applicants should clearly identify their proficiency with relevant Microsoft and Google Workspace applications.

Where appropriate, mention specific tools rather than simply writing “computer literate.”

Application Deadline

The official City of Boston posting lists the application deadline as January 29, 2027.

Applicants are encouraged to review the official vacancy carefully and submit their application before the closing date.

How to Apply

Applications are submitted through the City of Boston’s official careers platform.

Interested candidates should review the complete vacancy requirements and use the official application option provided on the posting.

Applicants should rely on the official City of Boston vacancy for the most current information concerning eligibility, application procedures and closing dates.

APPLY HERE

Important Points to Remember Before Applying

Before submitting an application, prospective candidates should confirm that they:

  • Meet the minimum experience requirement or qualify under the degree substitution provision.
  • Have a bachelor’s degree if available, noting that it is strongly preferred.
  • Can demonstrate strong organizational and communication skills.
  • Have an interest in public service, civic engagement or youth programmes.
  • Can work effectively with diverse communities.
  • Are able to manage several projects at the same time.
  • Are prepared to work some evenings and weekends.
  • Can travel to off-site locations when required.
  • Have proficiency with Microsoft applications and Google Suite.
  • Understand that bilingual ability is preferred.
  • Understand that a driver’s licence is preferred.
  • Can satisfy the required C.O.R.I. and S.O.R.I. checks.
  • Meet the Boston residency requirement.
  • Can commit to a one-year rotating position.
  • Submit the application before January 29, 2027.

Visit HERE for more information about the City of Boston Special Projects Fellow 2026–2027.

Conclusion

The City of Boston Special Projects Fellow position offers an opportunity to gain practical experience in municipal government while contributing to programmes designed to strengthen youth engagement, civic participation and community development.

The role is broader than a traditional administrative fellowship because the successful candidate will combine project management, stakeholder engagement, youth outreach, communications, event support, logistics, budget tracking and community collaboration. It is therefore particularly suitable for an organized professional who enjoys working across different projects and engaging directly with communities.

The position provides exposure to the work of the Office of Youth Engagement and Advancement and its efforts to ensure that young people have access to resources, opportunities and platforms through which they can participate in their communities and become leaders.

However, prospective applicants should pay especially close attention to the Boston residency requirement. While the City of Boston emphasizes equal opportunity and diversity in its hiring practices, residency is separately identified as a mandatory condition for this position. Candidates should therefore verify that they satisfy this requirement before investing significant time in an application.

With a salary of $25 per hour, a 35-hour workweek and a one-year term, the position could provide valuable practical exposure to public-sector project management and youth engagement. Applications must be submitted by January 29, 2027.

Geographic eligibility: Boston residency is required. The posting’s equal-opportunity policy states that qualified applicants are considered without discrimination based on race, national origin and other protected characteristics, but this does not waive the Boston residency requirement.

Deadline: January 29, 2027
