item.content:encoded:
The Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters (EMJM) programme offers an exceptional opportunity for students from around the world to pursue an international master’s degree through a consortium of universities located in different countries.

Unlike a conventional master’s programme where students may remain at one university for the entire duration of their studies, Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters are designed around international mobility. Students typically study at several universities and may also participate in research projects, traineeships, fieldwork, thesis preparation and other academic activities in different countries.

The programme is supported by the European Union’s Erasmus+ programme, and selected master’s programmes can provide highly competitive scholarships to the best-ranked applicants worldwide. Depending on the individual programme, scholarships can contribute toward participation costs as well as travel, visa and living expenses.

For students seeking an internationally recognised master’s degree, exposure to different academic systems, multicultural learning environments and international professional networks, Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters can be one of the most valuable study opportunities available.

Opportunity Category

Scholarship / International Master’s Degree Programme

The Erasmus Mundus opportunity combines postgraduate study with competitive scholarship funding. Students apply to individual Erasmus Mundus Joint Master programmes rather than submitting one general application to Erasmus Mundus.

What Are Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters?

Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters are prestigious international master’s programmes that are jointly designed and delivered by a consortium of higher education institutions.

A participating programme normally brings together at least three higher education institutions from at least three different countries. The consortium may also include associated partners from academic, research, professional, governmental, business or other non-academic sectors.

This structure gives students the opportunity to experience higher education across different countries and institutions while completing one coordinated master’s programme.

Depending on the programme, students may move between participating universities during their studies. The exact mobility pathway varies from one master’s programme to another, so prospective applicants should carefully examine the official programme website before applying.

Why Study an Erasmus Mundus Joint Master?

There are several reasons why Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters are attractive to international students.

1. Study in multiple countries

One of the defining characteristics of an Erasmus Mundus Joint Master is international mobility.

Rather than completing the entire programme at one university, students may spend different parts of their master’s degree at different institutions within the consortium.

This can expose students to:

  • Different European higher education systems
  • International academic perspectives
  • Multiple research environments
  • Different cultures and languages
  • International professional networks
  • Diverse student communities
  • Cross-border approaches to research and problem-solving

The specific countries and universities involved depend on the master’s programme selected.

2. International academic experience

Erasmus Mundus programmes bring together students and academics from different parts of the world.

Studying in such an environment can help students develop a broader understanding of their academic discipline while learning to work with people from different cultural and professional backgrounds.

This can be particularly valuable for graduates interested in international development, public policy, communication, science, technology, environmental studies, business, social sciences and other disciplines where international collaboration is important.

3. Prestigious master’s programmes

Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters are developed and delivered by international university consortia.

The participating institutions work together to create an integrated programme rather than simply offering separate courses under a common name.

Students therefore receive an academic experience built around collaboration between the participating institutions.

4. Opportunities for research and practical experience

An Erasmus Mundus Joint Master is not necessarily limited to traditional classroom-based learning.

Depending on the programme, students can undertake:

  • Academic coursework
  • Research activities
  • Traineeships
  • Practical projects
  • Fieldwork
  • Thesis preparation
  • Master’s thesis research
  • Thesis defence

The exact combination varies according to the selected programme.

This makes it important for applicants to examine individual programme curricula before deciding which Erasmus Mundus master’s programme best matches their academic and professional objectives.

Erasmus Mundus Scholarships

One of the most attractive features of the programme is the availability of competitive scholarships.

Some Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters offer full scholarships to the best-ranked students worldwide.

Scholarship arrangements vary according to the specific programme and the applicable funding rules. However, the official Erasmus Mundus information indicates that scholarships can cover or contribute toward major costs associated with participating in the master’s programme.

Potential areas of financial support include:

  • Participation or programme costs
  • Travel expenses
  • Visa-related expenses
  • Living allowance

Because funding conditions can differ between programmes and application cycles, applicants should not assume that every Erasmus Mundus master’s programme provides exactly the same scholarship package.

The individual master’s programme website should always be checked for the current scholarship amount, eligibility conditions, payment arrangements and covered expenses.

How Long Are Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters?

Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters generally last between one and two academic years.

Programmes can comprise:

  • 60 ECTS credits
  • 90 ECTS credits
  • 120 ECTS credits

The duration depends on the specific master’s programme.

Applicants should therefore examine the programme description carefully to determine:

  • Programme duration
  • Number of semesters
  • Required mobility periods
  • Participating universities
  • Study locations
  • Internship or traineeship requirements
  • Research requirements
  • Thesis requirements
  • Graduation arrangements

What Degree Will You Receive?

Students who successfully complete an Erasmus Mundus Joint Master may receive either a joint degree or multiple degrees, depending on the structure of the programme.

Joint degree

A joint degree is a single degree certificate issued on behalf of at least two higher education institutions within the consortium.

Multiple degrees

A multiple-degree arrangement means that the student receives at least two degree certificates from two higher education institutions belonging to the consortium.

The precise degree arrangement is established by the individual Erasmus Mundus Joint Master.

Students should therefore review the degree structure before applying and understand which institutions will award the qualification.

Who Can Apply for Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters?

Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters are designed for students from around the world.

The programme information states that students from all over the world are welcome to apply. Therefore, the opportunity is not restricted to applicants from European countries.

Applicants from Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, the Caribbean, Oceania and other regions may be eligible, provided they satisfy the requirements of the particular master’s programme they select.

However, international eligibility does not mean that every applicant automatically qualifies for every programme. Each Erasmus Mundus master’s programme establishes its own academic and admission requirements.

Academic Requirements

The general requirement is that applicants must:

  • Hold a bachelor’s degree or first degree; or
  • Be in the final year of their bachelor’s degree and graduate before the master’s programme begins.

Applicants may also qualify if they can demonstrate an equivalent level of learning.

Where an equivalent qualification is used, it must be officially recognised in accordance with the relevant national legislation and practices of the country where the degree is awarded.

This means prospective applicants should carefully verify whether their existing qualification is considered equivalent to a bachelor’s degree for their selected Erasmus Mundus programme.

Final-Year Bachelor’s Students

Students who have not yet completed their bachelor’s degree may still be able to apply.

However, applicants in their final year must graduate before the Erasmus Mundus Joint Master begins.

This is particularly important because applicants should not assume that being accepted while completing a bachelor’s degree means they can postpone graduation indefinitely.

Students should check the individual master’s programme for its specific documentation and graduation verification requirements.

Eligibility for Applicants from Africa

Students from African countries can apply to Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters.

There is no general restriction limiting the opportunity to European applicants. Applicants from African countries can compete for available places and scholarships alongside eligible applicants from other parts of the world.

For example, prospective applicants from countries such as:

  • Kenya
  • Uganda
  • Tanzania
  • Rwanda
  • Ethiopia
  • Ghana
  • Nigeria
  • South Africa
  • Zambia
  • Zimbabwe
  • Malawi
  • Botswana
  • Namibia
  • Senegal
  • Cameroon
  • Egypt
  • Morocco
  • Other African countries

may explore the available catalogue and determine whether they meet the admission requirements of individual programmes.

Nationality alone, however, does not guarantee admission or a scholarship. Academic qualifications and programme-specific eligibility requirements remain important.

Application Process

One of the most important things prospective applicants should understand is that there is not one universal application form for all Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters.

Students apply directly to the institution or consortium running their chosen programme.

The application process can therefore differ significantly from one master’s programme to another.

Step 1: Search the Erasmus Mundus catalogue

The first step is to explore the official Erasmus Mundus catalogue and identify master’s programmes relevant to your academic background and career objectives.

When searching the catalogue, applicants should pay attention to:

  • Programme title
  • Academic discipline
  • Participating universities
  • Participating countries
  • Programme duration
  • Mobility requirements
  • Admission requirements
  • Application deadline
  • Scholarship availability
  • Required documents
  • Language requirements

Step 2: Visit the master’s programme website

After identifying an interesting programme, applicants should visit its official programme website.

The programme website is the authoritative source for the specific admission requirements and application instructions.

Applicants should not rely solely on general Erasmus Mundus information because individual master’s programmes can have different requirements.

Step 3: Check the academic requirements

Applicants should determine whether their bachelor’s degree or equivalent qualification is accepted.

They should also review any programme-specific requirements relating to:

  • Academic discipline
  • Previous coursework
  • Grade requirements
  • Professional experience
  • Language proficiency
  • Research experience
  • Technical skills
  • Other qualifications

Step 4: Check scholarship requirements

If funding is important to you, determine whether the programme offers Erasmus Mundus scholarships and whether you need to complete any additional scholarship-related section of the application.

Some programmes may assess applicants for scholarships as part of the main application process, while others may provide specific instructions.

Step 5: Prepare the required documents

The exact documents vary by programme, but applicants should expect to provide some combination of:

  • Bachelor’s degree certificate
  • Academic transcripts
  • Proof of graduation or expected graduation
  • Curriculum vitae
  • Motivation letter
  • Proof of language proficiency, where required
  • Identification documents
  • Recommendation letters, where required
  • Other programme-specific supporting documents

Applicants should follow the official programme instructions carefully because submitting an incomplete application can affect eligibility.

Step 6: Submit before the programme deadline

Once the application is complete, submit it through the application system specified by the master’s programme.

Do not assume that there is one universal Erasmus Mundus deadline.

The deadline is determined by the individual programme.

When Is the Erasmus Mundus Application Deadline?

There is no single universal deadline for all Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters.

The official Erasmus Mundus information states that, in most cases, applications should be submitted between October and January for programmes beginning during the following academic year.

However, the exact deadline depends on the master’s programme.

Applicants should therefore check the official website of their selected programme for the precise application deadline.

Important deadline advice

Because many programmes have competitive scholarship selection processes, prospective students should begin preparing well before October.

Waiting until the final days of an application period can create problems if you need:

  • Academic transcripts
  • Recommendation letters
  • Language test results
  • Certified documents
  • Passport or identification documents
  • A strong motivation statement
  • Additional programme-specific documentation

Deadline: Generally October to January for programmes starting in the following academic year, but the exact deadline varies by master’s programme.

What Makes the Scholarship Competitive?

Erasmus Mundus scholarships are highly competitive because they are intended for the best-ranked applicants.

Applicants therefore need to do more than simply meet the minimum admission requirements.

A strong application should demonstrate a clear connection between the applicant’s:

  1. Academic background
  2. Professional or extracurricular experience
  3. Motivation for the chosen programme
  4. Career objectives
  5. Relevant skills
  6. Interest in the programme’s academic focus
  7. International or cross-cultural interests
  8. Potential contribution to the programme community

How to Strengthen Your Application

Research the programme carefully

Do not apply simply because a programme offers a scholarship.

Read the curriculum, mobility structure, research areas, participating universities and career outcomes.

Your motivation statement should demonstrate that you understand what the programme offers.

Match your background to the programme

Applicants should clearly explain how their previous academic and professional experiences prepare them for the master’s programme.

For example, if your bachelor’s degree is in communication, you should identify relevant communication, research, media, digital, development, public relations or related experience when applying to an appropriate programme.

Build a strong motivation statement

A strong motivation statement should explain:

  • Why you want to study the programme
  • Why the subject is important to you
  • Why you selected that particular Erasmus Mundus programme
  • What experience you bring
  • What you hope to learn
  • How the programme fits your career plans
  • What you intend to contribute after graduation

Avoid writing a generic statement that could be submitted to any university.

Demonstrate international motivation

Because Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters are inherently international, applicants should demonstrate their ability and willingness to learn and collaborate in multicultural environments.

International exposure can come from education, work, volunteering, research, community projects or other relevant experiences.

Start early

Applicants should begin preparing months before the deadline.

A useful preparation timeline could include:

Several months before applications open

  • Research programmes
  • Compare academic requirements
  • Identify suitable programmes
  • Review scholarship conditions

Before the application deadline

  • Prepare your CV
  • Draft your motivation letter
  • Request recommendation letters
  • Obtain academic documents
  • Check language requirements
  • Prepare any required tests

Before submission

  • Review every requirement
  • Check document formats
  • Proofread the application
  • Confirm the correct application portal
  • Submit before the deadline

Advice and Support for Applicants

Prospective applicants can also find resources through the Erasmus Mundus Association, which provides information and resources intended to help applicants understand the programmes and application process.

These resources can include programme contacts, events involving national volunteer representatives and stories from successful applicants.

Learning from previous applicants can help prospective students better understand the application process and prepare a stronger submission.

No Application date yet. In most cases, you should submit your application between October and January for courses starting the following academic year.

Erasmus Mundus in Numbers

The Erasmus Mundus programme has a substantial international track record.

According to the official Erasmus+ information referenced by the programme, almost 50,000 students have participated since 2004.

This long history demonstrates the scale and international reach of Erasmus Mundus and highlights the programme’s role in facilitating international postgraduate education.

Erasmus Mundus Opportunities Beyond Students

Although this opportunity is focused on students seeking master’s degrees, Erasmus+ also provides other forms of support.

Grants for higher education institutions

Erasmus+ provides grants to higher education institutions to develop and run Erasmus Mundus Joint Master programmes.

Institutions interested in participating should consult the official Erasmus+ information for organisations.

Opportunities for researchers

Researchers may also find related opportunities under the Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions, including postdoctoral fellowships and staff exchanges.

Other Erasmus+ opportunities

Erasmus+ also provides various opportunities and forms of support for students, staff and other eligible participants.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Erasmus Mundus available to students from Africa?

Yes. Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters welcome applications from students around the world. African students can apply provided they meet the requirements of the particular master’s programme.

Do I need to already have a master’s degree?

No. The general requirement is a bachelor’s degree or equivalent first degree. Students in the final year of their bachelor’s degree may also apply, provided they graduate before the master’s programme begins.

Can final-year undergraduate students apply?

Yes. Final-year bachelor’s students can apply, but they must complete and graduate from their bachelor’s programme before the Erasmus Mundus master’s programme begins.

Are Erasmus Mundus scholarships fully funded?

Some Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters offer full scholarships to the best-ranked students worldwide. Scholarship coverage can include participation costs and contributions toward travel, visa and living expenses. The exact funding package varies by programme.

Can I choose any university in Europe?

No. Applicants apply to specific Erasmus Mundus Joint Master programmes, each of which has its own consortium of participating universities. Students follow the mobility structure established by their chosen programme.

How many universities participate in an Erasmus Mundus Joint Master?

An Erasmus Mundus Joint Master normally involves at least three higher education institutions from at least three different countries, together with associated partners.

How long does an Erasmus Mundus master’s degree take?

The programmes generally last between one and two academic years and may comprise 60, 90 or 120 ECTS credits.

Will I receive one degree or several degrees?

Depending on the programme, you may receive either a joint degree issued on behalf of multiple institutions or multiple degrees issued by two or more institutions in the consortium.

Is there one Erasmus Mundus application deadline?

No. Each master’s programme establishes its own deadline. In most cases, applications are submitted between October and January for programmes beginning in the following academic year.

Where do I apply?

You apply directly to the institution or consortium running the Erasmus Mundus Joint Master programme you have selected.

Where can I find available programmes?

You can search the official Erasmus Mundus catalogue for the latest programmes available.

Category Details

Study level Master’s
Funding Competitive scholarships available for selected programmes
Eligible applicants Students from around the world
General academic requirement Bachelor’s degree or equivalent
Final-year students Eligible if they graduate before the programme begins

Potential scholarship support Participation costs, travel, visa and living allowance

Typical application period October–January
Exact deadline Varies by programme

Visit HERE to learn more about the Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters Scholarships 2026–2027.

Conclusion

The Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters programme represents a major opportunity for international students seeking an advanced degree in a highly international academic environment.

With master’s programmes delivered by consortia of universities across different countries, students can gain international academic exposure, participate in research and practical activities, build cross-cultural networks and potentially earn a joint or multiple-degree qualification.

The availability of competitive scholarships makes the opportunity particularly attractive to students who may otherwise find international postgraduate study financially difficult. Selected scholarship recipients can receive support toward participation costs as well as travel, visa and living expenses, depending on the individual programme.

However, prospective applicants should remember that Erasmus Mundus is not a single master’s course with one universal application deadline. The programme consists of numerous individual Joint Masters, each with its own participating universities, academic focus, admission criteria, scholarship arrangements and application deadline.

The best strategy is therefore to begin early, search the official Erasmus Mundus catalogue, identify programmes that match your academic and career goals, study the individual programme requirements carefully and submit a well-prepared application directly through the appropriate programme.

For students with a bachelor’s degree or those approaching graduation who want to experience international postgraduate education, Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters can provide a pathway to study across multiple institutions and countries while becoming part of a global academic community.

item.content:encoded:
We Are Not Waiting is a global youth-led initiative inviting young people who are already creating fairer, more sustainable and socially just futures to put their work on the record through an open-access anthology co-produced by The 50 Percent at the Club of Rome and the UNESCO–MOST BRIDGES UK Hub.

The initiative is calling on young practitioners aged 14 to 35 who are actively working to transform communities and systems through areas such as regenerative economics, climate justice, circular living, peacebuilding, mutual aid, art, culture and storytelling.

Rather than focusing only on theories about what a better future could look like, We Are Not Waiting seeks to document what young people are already doing in practice. Across communities worldwide, young people are organising, restoring ecosystems, developing alternative economic models, creating networks of solidarity, strengthening social cohesion, using creativity to challenge dominant narratives and finding new approaches to persistent social and environmental problems.

Applicants do not need to be academics, professional researchers or established writers. The organisers are specifically interested in lived experience, practical action and original perspectives from young people who are actively engaged in the work they want to write about.

Interested participants must submit an abstract of no more than 500 words by 31 August 2026. Approximately 18 contributions are expected to form the final anthology. Applicants whose abstracts are selected will be invited to develop their ideas into full contributions of approximately 2,000 words, with editorial support provided throughout the writing process.

The resulting open-access anthology will contain six chapters covering six major themes of systems change, with the project aiming to launch the publication at the UNESCO MOST Forum 2027.

About the We Are Not Waiting Initiative

We Are Not Waiting: Amplifying Youth-Led Initiatives for Systems Change is designed around a simple but important idea: young people are not merely waiting for governments, institutions or established leaders to create solutions to the world’s interconnected challenges.

They are already building alternatives.

The project centres young people aged 14–35 as designers and practitioners of alternative systems that are already in motion. It aims to showcase real-world initiatives and create a durable record of how youth-led systems change is happening in communities.

The initiative has two major components:

  1. An open-access anthology comprising six chapters across six themes, with the aim of launching at the UNESCO MOST Forum 2027.
  2. A webinar series exploring the six themes through one question-and-answer session and two youth-led thematic sessions.

At the heart of the project is the anthology, which is intended to be much more than a traditional collection of essays. It will serve as a policy-relevant record of youth-led systems change grounded in practical experiences.

What Makes the We Are Not Waiting Anthology Different?

The anthology is being deliberately designed to place young people’s knowledge, experiences and perspectives at its centre.

Three characteristics distinguish the publication:

  • It is written, reviewed and edited by young people themselves.
  • It is grounded in real-world practice rather than abstract discussion alone.
  • It will be published in an open-access format, making the resulting knowledge accessible to a wider audience.

The project provides young practitioners with an opportunity to document what they have learned through their initiatives while contributing to broader conversations about systemic change, social transformation and innovation.

Who Can Submit an Abstract?

The call is open to anyone aged 14 to 35 at the time of submission who is actively engaged in work connected to at least one of the anthology’s six themes.

Applicants do not need:

  • Academic credentials;
  • An institutional affiliation;
  • To be professional researchers;
  • To be established writers; or
  • To have definitive solutions to the challenges they are addressing.

Instead, the central requirement is that the proposed contribution must be grounded in genuine lived experience and real engagement with the issue or initiative being discussed.

Applicants may submit either:

  • Individually, or
  • As part of a small team.

For team submissions, all contributing authors must satisfy the 14–35 age requirement.

The organisers particularly encourage contributions from the Global Majority and indigenous communities, helping ensure that perspectives and knowledge systems that may be underrepresented in conventional academic and policy discussions are included.

Special Submission Requirement for Applicants Aged 18 and Under

There is an additional submission procedure for younger participants.

If an entrant is 18 years old or younger, their submission must be made on their behalf by an adult, such as:

  • A parent;
  • A guardian; or
  • A teacher.

The submission should include the young entrant’s details together with the adult’s contact information.

This does not change the emphasis on the young person’s ideas and experience; it is a procedural requirement for submitting the application.

What Should You Submit?

Applicants are invited to submit an abstract of no more than 500 words.

The abstract should be written in the applicant’s own voice using clear and accessible language. Academic or highly technical terminology is not required.

The organisers want submissions that communicate real experiences and original thinking rather than attempting to sound like conventional academic papers.

A strong abstract should address four key areas.

1. Describe Your Initiative, Project or Practice

Explain the initiative, project, activity, network or practice that you want to write about.

Applicants should provide enough context for reviewers to understand:

  • What the work involves;
  • Where or within what context it operates;
  • What issue it seeks to address;
  • Who is involved; and
  • What the applicant’s connection to the initiative is.

2. Explain What Makes the Work Distinct

Applicants should explain what their work does differently.

Consider questions such as:

  • What conventional approach does the initiative challenge?
  • What does the work refuse or seek to change?
  • What alternative does it provide?
  • How does the initiative rethink an existing system or practice?

The objective is to demonstrate how the work contributes to creating or imagining different systems rather than merely reproducing existing approaches.

3. Ground the Contribution in Concrete Examples

The anthology is focused on practice.

Applicants should therefore show that their proposed full contribution will include real examples rather than relying exclusively on theoretical arguments.

This could include experiences from communities, projects, campaigns, organisations, networks, cultural initiatives, environmental actions or other practical work.

4. Reflect on Learning and Broader Systems Change

Applicants should also explain what they and their communities have learned through the work.

The abstract should indicate how the initiative has contributed, or could contribute, to broader systemic change.

The focus is therefore not simply on describing an activity but on examining what that activity reveals about how systems can be challenged, repaired, redesigned or transformed.

Six Themes for the We Are Not Waiting Anthology

Applicants must connect their abstract to one of six major themes.

Theme 1: Re-weaving the Future — Networks and Economies That Make the World Anew

This theme focuses on regenerative economics and community-centred alternatives to conventional economic systems.

The organisers are interested in projects and practices demonstrating how young people are redesigning systems involving:

  • Exchange;
  • Value creation;
  • Resource sharing;
  • Community economies;
  • Regenerative approaches; and
  • Networks built around relationships and collective wellbeing.

The emphasis is on a relational rather than merely technical approach to economic transformation.

Young people who are experimenting with alternative economic systems, community-led resource models or regenerative approaches may find this theme particularly relevant.

Theme 2: Building Resilience Through Ecological Resistance and Restoration

This theme centres on climate justice, ecological resistance and environmental restoration.

The organisers are seeking stories and experiences that demonstrate how young people are defending, restoring and renewing the living world.

Relevant work may involve areas such as:

  • Climate justice activism;
  • Ecosystem restoration;
  • Community environmental action;
  • Ecological resistance;
  • Biodiversity protection;
  • Environmental justice; and
  • Relationships between communities and ecosystems.

The focus extends beyond simply managing environmental problems. Contributors are encouraged to reflect on what it means to actively defend and renew the living world.

Theme 3: Living Circular Futures — Small Changes, Big Difference

The third theme explores circular living and low-impact innovation.

The organisers are particularly interested in concrete and practice-oriented examples showing how people can adapt their ways of living, producing, consuming and sharing resources.

Contributions may explore change occurring at different levels, including:

  • Personal practices;
  • Community initiatives;
  • Local innovation;
  • Circular economic models;
  • Low-impact approaches; and
  • Broader systemic transformation.

Applicants should demonstrate what circularity looks like when translated from an idea into real-world practice.

Theme 4: Between Fracture and Repair — Youth-Led Peacebuilding and Social Cohesion

This theme examines the role young people play in peacebuilding and strengthening social cohesion.

It recognises that peace has both political and deeply personal dimensions.

Contributions may explore experiences involving:

  • Youth-led peacebuilding;
  • Community reconciliation;
  • Social cohesion;
  • Repairing fractured relationships;
  • Conflict transformation;
  • Freedom; and
  • Everyday practices that contribute to peace.

The organisers welcome work that examines both large-scale political realities and the everyday experiences through which fractured communities seek repair.

Theme 5: Communities of Care — Youth-Led Networks Built on Solidarity, Not Charity

The fifth theme focuses on mutual aid and community solidarity.

The anthology seeks contributions that demonstrate the distinction between mutual aid and conventional charitable giving.

The central editorial perspective is community over individuality.

Applicants could examine how young people are developing structures and networks of care that:

  • Prioritise solidarity;
  • Strengthen communities;
  • Share resources;
  • Support collective wellbeing;
  • Build reciprocal relationships; and
  • Avoid reproducing dependency.

This theme is particularly relevant to young people working within community networks and grassroots initiatives where care is understood as a collective responsibility.

Theme 6: Stories That Move Systems — Art, Culture and Storytelling as Tools for Transformation

The final theme explores the role of art, culture, narrative and storytelling in systems change.

The organisers are seeking contributions showing how creative practices can actively shape transformation rather than simply illustrate social issues.

Relevant work could involve:

  • Visual art;
  • Cultural practice;
  • Storytelling;
  • Film;
  • Performance;
  • Literature;
  • Community narratives;
  • Creative campaigns; and
  • Other forms of cultural expression.

Applicants should demonstrate how creative practice or storytelling functions as an instrument for changing systems, perspectives, narratives or relationships.

What Happens If Your Abstract Is Selected?

Successful applicants will move from the abstract stage into development of the full anthology.

Selected authors will be invited to prepare a contribution of approximately 2,000 words.

Importantly, authors will not be expected to navigate the development process alone. The project’s editorial team will provide editorial support throughout the process, helping contributors develop their initial abstracts into full pieces suitable for publication.

This support is particularly significant because applicants do not need previous academic publishing or professional writing experience.

The intention is to enable practitioners with valuable lived experience to communicate what they have learned in a clear and accessible way.

The anthology is expected to bring together approximately 18 contributions from young practitioners.

These contributions will collectively cover the six themes and document different approaches to youth-led systems change.

By bringing these experiences together in one open-access publication, the project seeks to create a record that can contribute to discussions among young people, communities, researchers, institutions, practitioners and policymakers.

Important Guidance on Artificial Intelligence and LLM Use

Applicants should pay close attention to the project’s guidelines concerning artificial intelligence and large language models.

The organisers strongly emphasise that the call is designed to uncover original thinking, creativity and authentic perspectives from young practitioners.

For this reason, using AI language models to draft, substantially revise or generate sections of a submission is not advised.

The organisers explain that they expect to receive a large volume of submissions. Although AI-detection tools are imperfect, editors may recognise recurring patterns in language, tone and ideas that can cause an otherwise strong submission to appear less original or inspired.

According to the guidelines, submissions that appear to rely heavily on AI are therefore likely to receive a lower assessment than work produced without such use.

Limited AI Uses That Are Permitted

AI tools may be used for limited supporting purposes, including:

  • Checking grammar and spelling;
  • Formatting references;
  • Translating source material from languages other than English; and
  • Conducting initial literature searches, provided the information is subsequently independently verified.

Applicants who use AI in their contribution are required to include an AI declaration.

The declaration must identify:

  1. The AI model and version used;
  2. The purpose or purposes for which it was used; and
  3. Confirmation that relevant data and references have been independently checked and verified by the author or authors.

Applicants should therefore ensure that the ideas, experiences, arguments and core writing in their submission genuinely represent their own perspective.

How to Submit an Abstract

Applicants should first carefully review the programme information and Q&A guidance before preparing their abstract.

The submission process can be approached as follows:

  1. Confirm that you are aged 14–35 at the time of submission.
  2. Identify which of the six themes most closely relates to your work.
  3. Choose a real initiative, project or practice in which you are genuinely engaged.
  4. Prepare an abstract of no more than 500 words.
  5. Explain the initiative and its context.
  6. Describe what makes the work different from existing approaches.
  7. Show how the proposed contribution will use concrete examples.
  8. Reflect on what you and your community have learned and how the work relates to broader systems change.
  9. Write in your own clear and accessible voice.
  10. Review the project’s AI guidelines carefully.
  11. If AI has been used within the permitted parameters, include the required AI declaration.
  12. Submit the abstract through the official submission form before the deadline.

Applicants aged 18 or under should remember that an adult, such as a parent, guardian or teacher, must make the submission on their behalf and provide the required contact details.

The deadline to submit an abstract for the We Are Not Waiting youth-led systems change anthology is 31 August 2026.

Conclusion

The We Are Not Waiting 2026 call for abstracts is an opportunity for young people who are already creating change to document their experiences and bring practical youth-led solutions into wider conversations about the future of societies, economies, communities and ecosystems.

Instead of asking applicants to speculate about what young people might accomplish someday, the initiative focuses on what they are already building today.

Whether that work involves regenerating ecosystems, developing community-centred economies, experimenting with circular living, repairing social divisions, building networks of mutual aid or using art and storytelling to transform narratives, the anthology seeks contributions grounded in action and lived experience.

With no requirement for academic credentials, institutional affiliation or professional writing experience, the call creates space for young practitioners whose knowledge has emerged directly from doing the work. Selected applicants will have the opportunity to transform their initial abstracts into approximately 2,000-word contributions with editorial support and potentially have their experiences documented in an open-access anthology planned for launch at the UNESCO MOST Forum 2027.

Young changemakers aged 14–35 who are actively working within one of the six themes should review the official guidance, prepare a clear and original abstract in their own voice, and submit their work by 31 August 2026.
